The scores

What do IDS, Angle and Mechanism mean?

For each sample, imprintomeR takes the median methylation of the paternally and maternally methylated probes of a panel and subtracts the reference (0.5, or each probe’s median in the controls), giving a paternal deviation x and a maternal deviation y.

  • IDS (Imprinting Deviation Score) = √(x² + y²): how far the sample is from the reference. Magnitude only.
  • Angle = atan2(y, x), 0–360°: the direction of the shift.
  • Mechanism: the 45° sector the Angle falls in (Pat-Gain, Pat-Gain+Mat-Loss, Mat-Loss, …), or ROI (retention of imprinting) when IDS is below the cutoff.

These describe bulk methylation along the annotated paternal and maternal axes. They are not parent-of-origin calls.

What does IDS mean with a control reference?

With the fixed 0.5 reference, IDS is the distance from perfect hemimethylation. With reference_group (in-cohort controls) or reference_beta (external controls), it is the distance from the controls: a related but different quantity. Use a control reference whenever tissue-matched controls exist; normal tissue rarely sits exactly at 0.5.

Which panel should I use?

Question Panel
11p15 (IC1/IC2) disturbance, e.g. BWS, SRS, Wilms tumor chr11p15: its paternal axis is IC1 (H19/IGF2), its maternal axis IC2 (KCNQ1OT1)
GNAS (20q13) chr20q13
Genome-wide imprinting, UPD, androgenetic/parthenogenetic samples selected (gametic ICRs by default)
Which ICRs are altered, multi-locus pattern selected with per-ICR scores (icr = TRUE, CLI --icr)

Caution for the selected panel: its paternal gametic axis has only two ICRs (H19/IGF2 with about 43 probes on EPIC, and IGF2 alt-TSS with one), so the sample-level paternal axis is essentially an 11p15 readout, and ICR-level resampling of that axis is unstable (see Why are my selected-panel intervals so wide?).

Choosing a cutoff

Is IDS 0.2 the right cutoff?

0.2 is the package default and an exploratory screening convention, not a calibrated diagnostic threshold. Whether it suits your data depends on where your controls lie.

  1. Look at the controls first. Plot or list the control IDS values. If nearly all controls lie below 0.2 with some margin, 0.2 is a reasonable starting point; if several controls approach or exceed it, it is too low for that tissue and panel.

  2. Derive control-based cutoffs with CalibrateIDS():

    cal <- CalibrateIDS(results, controls = "control", method = "quantile", probs = 0.99)
# adds IDS_z (robust z), IDS_control_percentile and Status_calibrated

    method = "max" uses the highest control; method = "youden" needs labelled cases.

  3. Report a sensitivity range, not one number: the number of cases above the cutoff for the range of control-based cutoffs (for example the 95th percentile, the maximum, and the maximum without outlier controls), alongside the count at 0.2.

  4. If you have molecular labels (MS-MLPA, copy number/LOH, methylation-specific PCR) for some samples, choose the cutoff with method = "youden", cases = …; that is the only way to calibrate it against truth.

How many controls do I need?

  • At least 5 tissue-matched controls for a control reference (with fewer than 3, the fixed 0.5 is used with a warning).
  • At least 10 for stable per-ICR z-scores (the package warns below 10).
  • With fewer than about 20, a “99th percentile” of controls is effectively the maximum and moves with every control added or removed; prefer the sensitivity range above.

What if some controls look abnormal?

Every control is scored leave-one-out, but each one still enters the reference for all other samples. List controls with IDS ≥ cutoff or a multi-locus flag, check them (adjacency to or contamination by tumor, batch, array plate, QC), and rerun with them excluded from the reference. A “normal” tissue sample that shows the same per-ICR pattern as the cases deserves particular scrutiny.

Is there a natural break in the data I can use?

Rarely. Case IDS values are usually continuous, often with several peaks but no gap near the cutoff. Do not pick a cutoff by eye from a histogram of cases.

Uncertainty

How do I get confidence intervals?

From R, or with the --n-boot and --n-perm options of the command-line script (see the command-line guide):

x <- readRDS("<prefix>_<genome>_imprintomeSet.rds")
x <- runImprintome(x, probeset = "chr11p15", reference_group = "control",
                   n_boot = 2000, resample_reference = TRUE, seed = 1,
                   result_name = "AnalyzeImprintStatus.chr11p15.boot")
res <- results(x)[["AnalyzeImprintStatus.chr11p15.boot"]]

This adds IDS_lower, IDS_upper, Angle_lower, Angle_upper and Mechanism_support; IDS and Mechanism themselves do not change. Use resample_reference = TRUE whenever controls are used, so the interval includes the uncertainty of the reference. A few thousand replicates of several hundred samples take seconds.

How should I call individual samples?

Use the interval, not just the point estimate:

Interval Call
IDS_lower ≥ cutoff above cutoff
IDS_upper < cutoff below cutoff
spans the cutoff borderline

Report the number of borderline samples; near the cutoff it is often large.

Why are my selected-panel intervals so wide?

The default resampling (resample = "icr") draws ICRs, then probes within them. With very few ICRs in a parental class (the selected panel’s paternal axis: two ICRs, one with a single probe), some replicates rest on one probe, which widens the interval considerably. Probe resampling (resample = "probe") is too narrow, because it treats correlated probes as independent; the truth lies in between. Use the chr11p15 panel for 11p15 conclusions and report selected-panel intervals descriptively.

Can I use Mechanism_support as a cutoff instead of IDS?

No. Mechanism_support is the fraction of bootstrap replicates that keep the sample’s sector. It measures how stable the direction label is, not how abnormal the sample is:

  • normal samples have the highest support, because their ROI label is stable;
  • support is lowest just above the IDS cutoff, because ROI is itself defined by the cutoff;
  • strongly abnormal samples whose Angle lies near a sector boundary have low support, although their IDS interval is far above the cutoff.

Use it as a second step: decide “abnormal or not” with IDS (preferably IDS_lower), then report the Mechanism only when Mechanism_support ≥ 0.8; otherwise describe the sample as “between sectors” (for example “Pat-Gain / Pat-Gain+Mat-Loss”).

What about the origin-permutation p-value?

n_perm tests whether a sample’s deviation depends on the annotated parental origin (a shift shared by both axes is not significant). It is exploratory: probe-level permutation is anti-conservative (p ≤ 0.05 in 34% of 122 benchmark controls), ICR-level permutation is the default (0% of the same controls), and with few ICRs the smallest attainable p is large. It needs a control reference.

Should I use the Confidence column?

Only as a coarse screening band. Confidence relabels IDS with fixed bands (< 0.1 “High (Normal)”, 0.1–0.2 “Low (Normal)”, 0.2–0.4 “Moderate (Alteration)”, ≥ 0.4 “High (Alteration)”); their sensitivity and specificity are reported in the threshold-selection benchmark. The bands ignore the number of probes, the controls, the tissue and resampling, and they do not change with ids_cutoff, so “High” is not a statement of statistical certainty: bootstrap intervals of samples labelled “High” often extend into the neighbouring band. For a call that accounts for uncertainty, use the interval-based call above (Status_interval, reported with n_boot) or CalibrateIDS().

Per-ICR results

How is an ICR called altered?

Each ICR with at least 3 probes is scored: deviation d = median(beta − reference) over its probes, z = (d − median of control d) / max(SD of control d, 0.02), with controls scored leave-one-out. An ICR is altered when |d| ≥ 0.175 and |z| ≥ 2, in either direction. These defaults were selected under a prespecified protocol in version 1.5.3; earlier versions used 0.075 and 3, so check the package version that produced your tables.

How should I read IC1/IC2 calls on chr11p15?

Pattern Usual reading (confirm with copy number or allelic data)
IC1 gain + IC2 loss paternal UPD11 / 11p15 LOH
IC1 gain only H19/IGF2 hypermethylation (IGF2 loss of imprinting)
IC2 loss only KCNQ1OT1 loss of methylation
neither no 11p15 methylation defect detected at these thresholds

What does the multi-locus (MLID) flag mean?

A sample is flagged when altered ICRs lie on at least two chromosomes (VTRNA2-1, polymorphic, is excluded). It is an algorithmic summary, not a diagnosis.

  • In blood with same-study controls it tracked array-defined MLID (benchmark GSE78773: 16/21 MLID, 2/16 single-locus, 0/39 controls flagged).
  • In tumor tissue it mostly reflects somatic methylation change and can be set in most tumors, and in some normal tissue samples too. Always report the flag rate in the controls next to it, and confirm constitutional MLID in blood or germline DNA.
  • With controls from another study, batch offsets produce spurious multi-locus calls; use same-study, same-processing controls.

Do sample-level IDS calls agree with the per-ICR calls?

On chr11p15, compare “IDS ≥ cutoff” with “has an IC1 or IC2 call” across a range of cutoffs: lower cutoffs flag samples without a per-ICR call, higher cutoffs miss samples that have one. Both use the same probes, so agreement shows consistency, not validation. For locus-level conclusions, prefer the per-ICR calls.

Practical questions

My beta file is too large to load

The panels use few probes (chr11p15: 82, selected: 782; fewer are present on a given array). Extract those rows first, with probe IDs from probesets_hg38.rds, then run on the subset; the scores are identical:

ps <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "probesets_hg38.rds", package = "imprintomeR"))
writeLines(as.character(as.data.frame(ps[["chr11p15"]])$NAME), "chr11p15_probes.txt")
{ head -1 beta.txt; grep -F -w -f chr11p15_probes.txt beta.txt; } > beta_chr11p15.txt

A multi-gigabyte beta matrix then runs in seconds and in little memory.

How do I make a readable per-ICR heatmap for hundreds of samples? 

p <- PlotICRHeatmap(icr_table, title = "Per-ICR deviation")
ggplot2::ggsave("icr_heatmap_large.jpg", p, width = 8,
                height = max(10, 0.12 * length(unique(icr_table$Sample_Name)) + 4),
                dpi = 200, limitsize = FALSE)

limitsize = FALSE allows images taller than 50 in. For the selected panel use a width of about 0.3 in per ICR + 4 in.

A reference group with a space in its name is not found

When the command is stored in a shell variable, run it with eval "$cmd" (or bsub … "$cmd"); a bare $cmd splits a value such as "Normal Kidney" into two words.

The command-line run ends with a differing number of rows error

In 1.5.3, run_imprintomeR.R without --icr could end with arguments imply differing number of rows: 2, 3, 1 after all results had been written. The results were complete; the message is fixed in 1.6.0 (with 1.5.3, add --icr to avoid it).
